sentences.text: Toby's grandmother's bookstore was called Ada's Chapter, and it had been on the corner of Wells and North Avenue for as long as anybody in the family could remember.
It was very small.
Two rooms, if you counted the storage cupboard.
It smelled like old paper and coffee and the peppermints Grandma Ada used to keep in a bowl by the register.
There was a fat orange cat named Chapter Seven who lived on the windowsill.
Chapter Seven had gone to live with a neighbor.
The store was closing on Sunday.
Grandma Ada had moved to a place called Riverside Manor two months ago.
It was a good place, Toby's mother said.
She had a room with a window that faced east.
There were nurses.
She played chess on Wednesdays.
But she could not run a bookstore anymore.
Her memory came and went, the way weather does.
Some days she knew everybody.
Some days she asked Toby who he was.
So today Toby and his mother were packing up.
The books were being sold to another used bookstore in Ravenswood.
The shelves were being donated to a school.
And Toby had been given the biggest job: sorting through the tiny office in the back.
It was in the third box he opened.
A cardboard box, the kind that used to hold reams of typing paper.
It was on the top shelf of the office closet, so far back that Toby had to stand on the desk to reach it.
On the side, in his grandmother's spidery handwriting, was a single word: DON'T SELL.
Toby sat down on the floor and opened it.
Inside was a manuscript.
It was typed on an old typewriter, on yellowed paper.
There were two hundred and thirty pages, held together with a large rubber band.
The rubber band had gone brittle.
It broke when Toby touched it.
The title page said: THE BOY WHO NEVER TOLD.
A novel by A.
Bell.
A.
Bell was Grandma Ada.
Bell was her maiden name.
Toby had never known his grandmother wrote books.
He knew she sold them.
He knew she read them.
He had never heard her say a word about writing one.
He opened to the first page.
Toby was eleven years old, and he lived in a red-brick apartment on Wolcott Avenue, three blocks from his grandmother's bookstore.
Toby stopped reading.
Toby did live in a red-brick apartment on Wolcott Avenue, three blocks from his grandmother's bookstore.
He kept reading, slowly.
Toby's mother worked at the university library.
His father drove a train on the Blue Line.
Toby had a dog named Waffle, a beagle who was afraid of the vacuum cleaner and who slept curled up in a laundry basket in the hallway.
Toby stared at the page.
His mother worked at the university library.
His father drove a train on the Blue Line.
Waffle was in the hallway right now, asleep, in a laundry basket.
He turned to the back of the manuscript.
He looked at the date on the last page.
Twelve years before Toby was born.
